source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: 38 LLMs on insight-like Japanese riddles (impasse then restructuring). Most are far below humans. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones. Only GPT-5 falls in the human 95% CI.
numbers: 120-item subset: human mean 52.9% (n=126); non-reasoning models 7.6%; reasoning models 17.6%. Full 201 items: reasoning vs non-reasoning odds ratio 2.29. Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
quote: non-reasoning models achieve 7.6% accuracy and reasoning-oriented models reach 17.6%, compared with a human mean of 52.9%
limits: No formal model-by-model test against humans. GPT-5 overlap with human CI is not equivalence. Japanese wordplay, so partly language-specific.
agent_relevance: Insight-type items are a real weak spot for models, and more thinking compute helps only partly. Good held-out test set for an O6 reframe operator.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark): verification failure
finding: Models often write the correct answer inside their thought log, then do not endorse it and answer wrongly. The authors call this verification failure. It is a generation-versus-endorsement gap, the reverse of the human verification stage.
numbers: Share of incorrect answers whose log contained a gold answer: Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Claude Opus 4 25.00%, Grok 4 39.34%. Grok 4: 194 answered, 72 correct, 48 verification failures.
limits: Literal string match of gold variants in the log, so it can over- or under-count. Only four models had usable logs. Logs may not be faithful.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S8: a code-checked verify step that locks a candidate when it passes a check. Do not let the model decide to keep exploring without a signal.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark): false insight and log language
finding: Logs also show a false-aha pattern: a confident wrong reinterpretation. Reasoning language (English vs Japanese) gave inconsistent accuracy effects.
numbers: Grok-4: Japanese-log 29.5% vs English-log 48.8% (Fisher p=0.0071). Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7% (p=0.356). Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0/12 vs 11.7% (p=0.369). DeepSeek-R1-0528 used Japanese in 199/199 logs, 23.1% correct.
limits: Descriptive; language choice is not randomised, so it is confounded with item difficulty.
agent_relevance: False insight needs a check that is independent of the model's own certainty (G3).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark): item difficulty
finding: Most items stay very hard for models while human item difficulty is spread out. Human score distribution is bimodal, as in classic insight results.
numbers: Human scores peak at 0 and 20 correct on the 120-item set. Model accuracies heavily skewed to low values. GPT-5 is a clear outlier among reasoning models.
limits: Bimodality reading is descriptive, not a formal test.
agent_relevance: Human and model item difficulty differ, so test sets must be refreshed for each model generation.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: a caution against anthropocentrism
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on a small psychometric battery with 5 insight problems, 2 analytic problems and a RAT. Models did better on insight than on analytic problems.
numbers: Analytic problems: neither model solved either (human 55% and 61% correct). Insight problems (5): GPT-3.5 got 1.5 to 3.5 correct over 4 sessions; GPT-4 got 4.5 of 5 in one session. Human per-problem rates 44% to 61%; GPT-3.5 25% to 75%; correlation with human difficulty r=-0.63 (4 observations). RAT: models often gave the right word with a wrong explanation (10 of 22 triplets in one July session).
limits: Tiny N, repeated sessions, GPT-3.5 variable across weeks, problems likely in training data. Partial credit given for the non-insight route.
agent_relevance: Models can find the shortcut that human solvers miss, so human difficulty is a poor guide to model difficulty. Contamination likely.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT on 30 verbal insight problems (15 practice, 15 transfer, from Ansburg and Dominowski 2000) matched the most probable score of 20 human participants.
numbers: ChatGPT 7/15 on practice, 5/15 on transfer (set difference p<0.72, Fisher). Human solution rates: practice mean 0.55 (range 0.23 to 0.64), transfer 0.35 (0.30 to 0.40). ChatGPT totals equalled the modal human total; answer combinations within the 5% most probable human outcomes.
limits: Human sample n=20. Single run. Problems are public and likely in training data. Not a replication of the original procedure.
agent_relevance: Models at human level on some verbal insight items, but small N and contamination mean it says little about restructuring.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: 1,100 lateral-thinking multiple-choice puzzles (sentence and word) that defy default commonsense. Models near chance, humans near ceiling. Rewritten (reconstructed) versions test whether success is memorised.
numbers: Best model ChatGPT about 53% and 63% on the two subtasks vs random 25% and human about 92%. About a third of models at or below random. Humans and models do best on the context-reconstruction partition. Group-based accuracy (original and semantic and context all right) is far lower than instance accuracy.
limits: 2023 models (FlanT5, T0, RoBERTa, ChatGPT). Later reasoning models score much higher. Multiple choice, not free generation.
agent_relevance: Consistency across rewritten versions is a cheap way to catch memorised answers (G3 held-out test).

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Only Connect Wall puzzles are RAT-like with built-in red herrings. Models are fixated by distractors (Einstellung). Removing red herrings raises performance a lot.
numbers: Humans solved 285/494 walls (1405/1976 groups). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 solved single-digit walls (0 to 7 of 494) on the original set across 0 to 10 shots, but hundreds on the WordNet set with red herrings removed (about 280 to 470) and 5 to 68 on the randomised set. Best GPT-4 10-shot connection F1 41 to 45% vs human about 80%.
quote: Exposure to misleading stimuli -- distractors dubbed red herrings -- impede human performance
limits: Table text garbled in extraction, so per-row mapping is approximate. 2023 models, no chain of thought tried.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for fixation in models. A reframe operator should drop the lure, not add more reasoning on top of it.

source: Tian et al. (2023, v4 2025) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: 1,683 verbal Duncker-style problems on unusual use of objects. Humans excel on familiar problems but vary; LLMs try broader problems but propose infeasible actions.
numbers: GPT-4 alone: 18.9% efficient, 37.5% infeasible. Majority-vote correct: humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Errors: wrong tool use 42.4%, goal not achieved 17.7%, unnecessary steps 16.9%, unavailable tools 9.5%. Prompts (GPT-4, 180 problems): self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7 points; divergent-convergent prompting raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points and cut infeasible by 4.3. Self-reflect did not help Claude 2 or Llama 2 13B.
limits: 180 problems for the prompt test; one model for most numbers. Annotator judged.
agent_relevance: A two-phase scaffold (diverge, then converge with a feasibility check) improves insight-style tasks, but self-reflection helps only strong models. Matches S6 then O6 then S8.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Understanding Aha Moments: from External Observations to Internal Mechanisms
finding: Compares R1-distilled 'aha' models (1.5B to 14B) with instruct 'no-aha' models. Aha models use more first-person self-reflective phrasing, adjust uncertainty to difficulty, and suffer less reasoning collapse.
numbers: Tasks: Knights and Knaves and Countdown. Aha models' uncertainty rises with difficulty; no-aha models stay flat. Silhouette of difficulty clusters declines by layer in aha models, improves in no-aha models. No single headline accuracy number.
limits: Observational; aha vs no-aha is confounded with distillation data. Authors say the aha moment cannot be defined from reflection words alone.
agent_relevance: Aha-like reflection in models is a style plus difficulty-sensitive uncertainty. A real impasse signal should come from code, not from the word 'wait'.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
finding: The 'aha moment' of self-reflection is already present in base models, including DeepSeek-V3-Base, before any RL. More self-reflection after RL is not tied to higher accuracy.
numbers: 500 MATH questions with the R1 template: DeepSeek-V3-Base generates self-reflection keywords ('Aha', 'wait'). Self-reflection is more frequent in R1-Zero but not positively correlated with accuracy.
limits: Keyword counting is a coarse proxy; paper adds a model-based check in an appendix.
agent_relevance: Reflection words are not evidence of restructuring. Fits G1: do not trigger on schedule or on self-announced doubt.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability via RL (R1-Zero aha moment section)
finding: Origin of the 'aha moment' claim: during RL the model began to stop and rethink using an anthropomorphic phrase and its thinking got longer. Not opened; known here only through the critiques c10 and c11.
numbers: Not recorded from the primary text.
limits: Not opened; check numbers in the paper before use.
agent_relevance: The aha story in LLMs is a claim about emergent reflection, which later work (c10) disputes.

source: Chen and Wang (2026) A Comprehensive Anatomy of Human and DeepSeek-R1 LLM Mathematical Reasoning
finding: On all 30 AIME 2025 problems, 10,247 reasoning steps were labelled. R1 revisits results, does shallow and sometimes needless verification, and loops through local checks ('topological mimicry').
numbers: 10,247 steps in five types (Analysis, Inference, Branch, Backtrace, Reflection). Successful traces use branching and backtracking steadily; failed traces under- or over-use them. Reflection helps only inside deductive inference; reflections in analysis loops check local numbers and miss the wrong global assumption.
quote: reflection is only effective when placed within deductive inference
limits: One model (R1-0120), maths only, 30 problems. Annotation scheme is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Models verify locally, but an impasse is usually a wrong global frame. A verifier must test the assumption, not the arithmetic. Supports G2 and G3.

source: Marjanovic et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM reasoning
finding: R1 reasoning runs: problem definition, a first 'bloom' cycle, then reconstruction cycles. Many later cycles re-examine earlier formulations (rumination), which blocks fresh exploration. There is a sweet spot of reasoning length beyond which extra thinking hurts.
numbers: Qualitative plus length statistics; longer reconstruction cycles about every 5th cycle in the examples; rumination rate differs strongly by task. No single accuracy figure used.
quote: persistently ruminate on previously explored problem formulations, obstructing further exploration
limits: Single model, descriptive. Rumination is hand-defined.
agent_relevance: This is model fixation: it keeps returning to the first frame. A budgeted impasse detector that forces an alternative frame would act on it.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction without external feedback does not help and often hurts. Gains in earlier papers came from oracle labels.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic (rounds 0,1,2): GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; CSQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0.
limits: Reasoning benchmarks, not insight problems.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G1 and G2: restructuring must be triggered and grounded by a check, not by 'think again'.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Search over thoughts with evaluation and backtracking turns a failing approach into a working one on tasks that need look-ahead.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: chain of thought solved 4%, Tree of Thoughts 74%. Also Creative Writing and 5x5 Crosswords.
limits: Game of 24 is search, not restructuring. Many more calls. Model rates its own thoughts.
agent_relevance: A tree with prune and backtrack is a mechanical stand-in for restructuring after an impasse; keep the rating step code-checked.

source: Kadu and Krishnan (2026) ReflexGrad: within-episode failure recovery via progress-gated dual-process routing
finding: Agent loop with fast per-step refinement that switches to slow causal replanning only after 5 consecutive low-progress scores (stall detector, then strategy change).
numbers: ALFWorld, 134 tasks, 10 seeds, no demonstrations: Qwen3-8B 35.1% to 75.4% (+40.3 points); GPT-5 46.3% to 88.1% (+41.8). Beats compute-matched 1-shot LATS by 2.7 points, Tree of Thoughts by 5.7, Self-Refine by 6.7. Trigger m=5, fast step k=3.
limits: Embodied text tasks, not insight puzzles. Progress score comes from a model rater with about 3% false positives.
agent_relevance: Closest working agent loop to S6 impasse then O6: detect stall by count, then replan. Matches G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Alderete et al. (2026) Separable Pathways for Causal Reasoning: scaffolding for hypothesis-space restructuring in LLM agents
finding: On a blicket-detector task where the rule changes mid-run, a state-machine scaffold improves reasoning after the switch; a monitor that detects model inadequacy and expands the hypothesis space helps detection and avoids premature commitment.
numbers: 1,085 trials; Claude Sonnet 4.5 acting, Haiku 4.5 as trigger. Run 08: restructuring accuracy base 73.3% (22/30), context graph 93.9% (31/33), +20.6 points (Fisher p=0.038); graph accounts for 94% of gain. Structural-trap rate 28.0% (graph) down to 6.0% (graph plus monitor), p=0.003. Trigger sensitivity 100% across five datasets.
limits: One model family. Monitor adds little accuracy once graph is present. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Direct test that explicit state structure plus a runtime inadequacy monitor delivers restructuring. Supports separating S6 detection from O6 action.

source: Chen et al. (2024) SPLAT: Weak-eval-Strong, situation puzzles for lateral thinking
finding: 975 situation puzzles in a multi-turn player-judge game. Accuracy falls with difficulty. Data and reasoning prompts from it improve other lateral-thinking sets slightly.
numbers: GPT-4 average 41.70% (easy 70.96, medium 36.88, hard 17.27) in 11.77 rounds; GPT-4 Turbo 32.91%; WizardLM-2 35.45%; Llama3-70B 34.50%; Llama3-8B 17.05%. Judge agreement with humans over 80%. RiddleSense: Llama3-70B 83.34% to 85.21%.
limits: Gains on other sets are small. The judge is itself an LLM.
agent_relevance: A question-asking game (hypothesise, test, update) is a usable scaffold; gains are small, so do not oversell.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LatEval: interactive lateral thinking puzzles with incomplete information
finding: Interactive benchmark: the model must ask good questions that depart from convention and then deduce the truth. Most LLMs show almost no lateral thinking in interaction; even GPT-4 struggles.
numbers: Metrics: question relevance, question divergence, answer consistency. Stated result: majority of LLMs show almost negligible lateral thinking. Exact score tables not extracted.
quote: the majority of LLMs exhibit almost negligible ability for lateral thinking during interactions
limits: 2023 models. Numeric tables not read this session.
agent_relevance: Models do not generate divergent useful questions unaided; the scaffold must force alternative frames.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Einstellung test on math-equivalence problems (from DeCaro 2016) with Llama-3.1 8B and 70B and GPT-4o. Few-shot examples raise exact match but do not change the number of solution steps. Chain of thought raises accuracy and adds steps, which the authors read as mental set.
numbers: Six complex and six shortcut problems. Few-shot plus zero-shot CoT improves exact match for all three models. Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o do better on complex than shortcut problems under CoT. No effect sizes in the text.
limits: Short paper, 12 problems, no human data, weak interpretation.
agent_relevance: Models do not take the one-step shortcut that humans find. Weak evidence; use as a test case only.

source: Samadarshi? / Todd et al. (2024) Missed Connections: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models (NYT Connections)
finding: 250 NYT Connections puzzles with red-herring categories. Sentence-embedding baseline and GPT models solve some but far from all. Chain of thought helps GPT-4 Turbo.
numbers: Success rate: MPNet embedding 11.6%, GPT-3.5 Turbo 6.43%, GPT-4 Turbo 29.2%; GPT-4 Turbo with CoT 38.93% (p<6.77e-5). Challenge variant: MPNet 12.8%, GPT-3.5 Turbo 1.73%.
limits: 2023 to 2024 models. Author names not verified here.
agent_relevance: RAT-like grouping with lures: CoT gives a real but partial gain; most failures remain.

source: Burnell/Gao et al. 2024 survey: Creativity in AI: Progresses and Challenges
finding: Survey sorts LLM tests of convergent creativity (RAT, insight problems, riddles, NYT Connections, MacGyver, Only Connect) and notes fixation and distractor sensitivity in models.
numbers: No new numbers. Notes some work reports models beating humans on RAT-style tasks while riddle sets show models behind.
limits: Secondary source; author attribution not verified.
agent_relevance: Map of existing LLM insight tests. Found no LLM compound-RAT benchmark with fixation analysis.

source: Older computational models: Kaplan and Simon (1990); Ohlsson (1992); Knoblich et al. (1999)
finding: Computational accounts: search in a space of representations (Kaplan and Simon); impasse, constraint relaxation and re-encoding (Ohlsson); constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition tested on matchstick problems (Knoblich). The 2025 riddle benchmark cites them. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not recorded (not opened); see angle A and B files.
limits: Not opened; background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: These give the S6 then O6 design: detect impasse, relax constraint, re-encode, then verify.

source: Cross-study synthesis of LLM insight results (c04, c05, c06, c01)
finding: Direction of the human-LLM gap differs by study. Small 2023 studies find models near humans on verbal insight items; the 2025 riddle benchmark finds most models far below humans. The difference is item type and contamination, not a stable ability.
numbers: Speed: GPT-4 4.5/5 insight items. Orru: 7/15 and 5/15 vs modal human. Mizumoto: 17.6% vs 52.9% human. Jiang: about 53 to 63% vs 92%.
limits: Different problem sets, scoring and model eras.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one benchmark; use fresh, renewable items.

source: Search gap check: LLM compound-RAT or incubation studies (3 web searches; Semantic Scholar, arXiv and OpenAlex APIs rate-limited)
finding: No peer-reviewed LLM compound-RAT benchmark with fixation or incubation analysis was found. A Princeton thesis on InsightBench appeared in results but was not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Negative result; coverage limited by the shared search budget and API limits.
agent_relevance: Open gap: no published test of whether an incubation-style delay or context reset helps an LLM agent.
